paragraphs: From what has gone before, it follows that the general will is always right and tends toward the public advantage. It does not follow, though, that the people’s deliberations are always equally correct. Our will is always for our own good, but we do not always see what that good is. The people is never corrupted, but it is often deceived, and only on those occasions does it seem to will what is bad.

There is often a great deal of difference between the will of all and the general will. The general will considers only the common interest, while the will of all takes private interest into account and is no more than a sum of particular wills. But take away from these same wills the pluses and minuses that cancel one another out,[1] and what remains as the sum of the differences is the general will.

Suppose the people, adequately informed, held its deliberations and the citizens had no communication with one another. Then the grand total of the small differences would always give the general will, and the decision would always be good. But when factions arise and partial associations form at the expense of the great association, the will of each of these associations becomes general in relation to its members while remaining particular in relation to the State. It may then be said that there are no longer as many votes as there are men, but only as many as there are associations. The differences become fewer and give a less general result. Finally, when one of these associations becomes so great that it prevails over all the rest, the result is no longer a sum of small differences but a single difference. In that case there is no longer a general will, and the opinion that prevails is purely particular.

It is therefore essential, if the general will is to be able to express itself, that there be no partial society within the State and that each citizen think only his own thoughts.[2] That was indeed the sublime and unique system established by the great Lycurgus. But if there are partial societies, it is best to have as many as possible and to keep them from being unequal, as Solon, Numa and Servius did. These precautions are the only ones that can guarantee that the general will is always enlightened and that the people in no way deceives itself.
